transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I can handle the technical parts fine, but I just can’t seem to keep all the pieces of these projects organized anymore. Since I got promoted to a lead architect role about a year ago, the sheer volume of different things I have to manage has just become too much to keep track of.

Have you noticed any difficulties with memory, learning new information, or making decisions since your promotion, or is it primarily the organization and management of tasks that's challenging for you?

Learning and making technical decisions are actually fine, it's really just the organization of everything that's killing me. Juggling roadmaps, code reviews, and demos feels like my head is a messy whiteboard where everything is half-erased. I keep jumping between tasks without a clear order and end up scrambling at the last minute to pull it all together.
Have you experienced any difficulties with focus, such as being easily distracted, or trouble sustaining attention on tasks, especially since taking on your new role?

Yes, keeping my focus has been a massive struggle since taking on this role a year ago. When I try to review design documents, the slightest thing like a Slack notification or someone walking past completely derails me. Even in meetings, my mind constantly drifts off to the point where colleagues have to ask if I'm still with them because I've completely lost track of the conversation.
Have you noticed any impulsive behaviors or actions since your promotion, such as interrupting others, blurting out answers, or acting on impulse without considering the consequences?

I haven't really noticed those kinds of impulsive behaviors like interrupting others or acting without thinking. My struggles are much more about trying to stay focused, keeping organized, and dealing with an internal restless feeling rather than acting impulsively.
Do you feel overwhelmed, anxious, or stressed when you're unable to organize tasks or stay focused, and does this affect your mood or overall sense of well-being?

I'm not quite sure how to describe its effect on my overall mood or well-being. Mostly, I just feel incredibly stressed when I'm scrambling to finish tasks at the last minute, and I've been really worried about my job security lately.

Can you tell me more about how you feel when you're not working or under pressure to meet deadlines, do you still experience difficulties with focus, restlessness, or feeling overwhelmed in your personal life or during leisure activities?

Yes, even during my personal time, I really struggle to sit quietly and focus on things I actually enjoy, like reading sci-fi or sketching. I'll find myself reading the same paragraph over and over, or I'll have to put on a podcast because pure silence makes me feel incredibly antsy within minutes.

Do you find that you're still able to enjoy activities you used to like, or has your interest in these activities decreased since you started experiencing these difficulties with focus and organization?

I definitely still have the interest and want to do them, but I just can't seem to sit quietly and immerse myself anymore. For instance, I'll try to read sci-fi but end up reading the same paragraph over and over, or I'll need a podcast playing because the silence makes me too antsy. My mind just constantly drifts off instead of letting me enjoy the activity in peace.
Do you often feel the need to be constantly on the move, fidget, or engage in activities that allow you to release excess energy, even when it's not necessarily required by the situation?

Yes, absolutely—during long Zoom calls, I get this restless buzz in my body that makes me constantly shift in my chair, pace off-camera, or fiddle with browser tabs to burn off energy. Even during quiet leisure activities like reading or sketching, I get so antsy in pure silence that I have to play a podcast just to cope with that feeling of being stuck.
Do you feel like you're enjoying things less than you used to, or is the issue more that you just can't focus long enough to enjoy them?

It's definitely not a lack of interest, as I still love reading sci-fi and sketching. The issue is purely that I can't focus long enough or sit quietly to actually immerse myself in them. I end up reading the same paragraph over and over, getting distracted by unrelated thoughts, or needing a podcast playing because pure silence makes me too antsy.
Did you experience difficulties with focus, restlessness, or organization during your childhood or adolescence, or have these issues primarily emerged since your promotion to the lead architect role?

While these problems have definitely gotten worse and more disruptive since my promotion a year ago, they actually go all the way back to my childhood. When I was in primary school, teachers always wrote on my report cards that I had "brilliant ideas but made careless mistakes." My parents even had to sit right next to me just to keep me focused enough to finish simple homework without drifting off.
Can you describe any specific behaviors from your childhood, such as fidgeting, running, climbing, or an inability to engage in activities quietly, that might have been indicative of hyperactivity?

I don't really recall having those kinds of hyperactive behaviors like climbing or running around excessively as a kid. My issues back then were much more about being scattered, losing focus, and constantly drifting off.
Did you ever have difficulties with waiting for your turn, interrupting others, or blurting out answers in class or during family discussions when you were a child?

I don't really recall having those specific issues with interrupting, waiting my turn, or blurting things out as a child. My struggles back then were much more about drifting off, losing track of things, and making careless mistakes.
Did you have any difficulties with following through on instructions, finishing homework, or completing chores as a child, and if so, how did your parents or teachers help you manage these tasks?

Yes, I had a lot of trouble finishing homework and staying on task as a child. My teachers often wrote on my report cards that I made careless mistakes despite having brilliant ideas. To get me through it, my parents had to physically sit with me just so I would finish simple assignments without constantly drifting off.

Have you experienced significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning as a result of your symptoms, such as problems with relationships, work performance, or daily life activities?

Yes, it has seriously hurt my work performance over the past year, leading to missed deliverables and frustrated teammates, which actually showed up in my last annual review. I've also started forgetting professional commitments like workshops and travel planning, which makes me look unreliable and has me really worried about my job security.

You mentioned that your symptoms have worsened since your promotion, but also recalled similar issues during childhood; can you clarify if you experienced any periods of significant improvement or remission of these symptoms between childhood and your current role?

I'm not really sure if I ever had a true period of remission. During my years as a regular coder, I think I just managed to cope because I could rely on deep-focus coding sprints to get by, but I don't know if that counts as a real improvement. Once my role changed and the administrative demands piled on, those coping mechanisms just stopped working.

Can you tell me more about how your symptoms changed or persisted from childhood through adolescence and into adulthood, and were there any specific factors or strategies that helped you manage them during different periods of your life?

I don't recall having any specific strategies during my adolescence other than just grinding to get through it. When I started my career, I managed to mask these attention difficulties by relying on deep-focus coding sprints, which worked well when my job was just writing code. Before that, it was just my parents sitting with me to finish tasks, so these issues have really been there the whole time.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood and have continued into adulthood, with some adaptation during certain periods. Can you estimate how often your symptoms of inattention and restlessness have caused significant problems in your daily life over the past six months?

It has been a constant, daily struggle over the past six months. Since taking on the lead architect role, these issues have ramped up to the point of causing significant problems almost every single day. The inattention, like missing API parameters or drifting off in meetings, and the restless buzz that makes me fidget during Zoom calls have directly led to concrete setbacks like missed deadlines, forgotten commitments, and a poor annual review.

You've described significant difficulties with inattention and restlessness, but can you compare the severity of these two issues for you - do you feel that your inability to focus and stay organized is more problematic, or is the restless, fidgety feeling equally or more disruptive to your daily life?

While the restless, fidgety feeling is uncomfortable, the inability to focus and stay organized is by far the more disruptive issue for me. The disorganization is what is actively hurting my job performance, causing missed deadlines, and threatening my job security. The restlessness is more of an internal buzz that I try to burn off, but the focus issues are what I really can't manage anymore.

Can you clarify if your current symptoms of inattention and restlessness are significantly worse now than they were in childhood, or have they remained relatively consistent, with the main difference being how they impact your life due to increased responsibilities?

The core symptoms of being scattered and losing track of details have actually been relatively consistent since childhood, when teachers noted my 'careless mistakes' and my parents had to sit with me to finish homework. However, they feel much more overwhelming now because my new lead architect role stripped away the deep-focus coding sprints that used to mask these issues. Replacing those sprints with heavy coordination and administrative tasks has made my symptoms highly visible and damaging to my performance.

You've mentioned that your symptoms have been present since childhood but have become more problematic with your new role. Can you specify if there was ever a period where you felt your symptoms were well-managed or if they have always been a source of difficulty for you?

I'd say they were relatively well-managed, or at least masked, during my years as a regular coder because I could rely on deep-focus coding sprints. While the underlying tendencies have always been there since childhood, that specific setup kept them from causing major issues. Once I got promoted to lead architect a year ago, that coping mechanism was stripped away, making them highly problematic.

Considering your symptoms have been present since childhood but have become more problematic with increased responsibilities, do you think the current issues are an exacerbation of longstanding tendencies or a new development triggered by your role change?

It is definitely an exacerbation of lifelong tendencies rather than a brand-new issue. I've had these scattered, lose-track-of-details struggles since primary school, but I was previously able to mask them through deep-focus coding sprints. The promotion to lead architect stripped away those coping mechanisms by introducing too many concurrent tasks and meetings, bringing these longstanding issues to the forefront.
Did you exhibit any symptoms of hyperactivity, such as fidgeting, running, or climbing, during adolescence or early adulthood that might have been less noticeable than your inattention symptoms?

I don't recall having any prominent physical hyperactivity symptoms like running, climbing, or excessive fidgeting during my adolescence or early adulthood. My difficulties have always felt much more related to attention and focus.

Can you describe how your symptoms have impacted your relationships with family and friends, and have you noticed any significant differences in how you interact with them now compared to before your promotion?

I haven't really noticed a significant impact on my relationships with family and friends. Since my promotion, my struggles and focus have been almost entirely centered on my professional life and managing my work commitments.

Looking back, did you often feel restless or have trouble engaging in quiet leisure activities as an adolescent or young adult, even if you didn't exhibit overt hyperactive behaviors like running or climbing?

I don't recall clearly if I felt that way or had trouble with quiet activities during my adolescence or young adulthood. Back then, my focus was mostly on just trying to get through my schoolwork, so I'm not really sure if I experienced that specific restlessness until much later in life.

Can you think of any times during your childhood or adolescence where you might have exhibited more subtle signs of hyperactivity, such as feeling internally restless or having trouble engaging in quiet activities, even if it wasn't as noticeable as running or climbing?

I don't really recall feeling internally restless or having trouble with quiet activities when I was younger. As far as I can remember, my childhood difficulties were mostly about drifting off, losing track of details, and making careless mistakes rather than physical or internal restlessness.

Can you think of any situations, either currently or in the past, where you felt the need to be constantly active, like tapping your hands or feet, or where you had trouble waiting for your turn, which might not have been as noticeable as other symptoms?

I definitely experience that physical restlessness now, especially during long Zoom calls where I'm mostly listening; I get this restless buzz and constantly shift in my chair, pace off-camera, or open new tabs just to burn off the feeling of being stuck. While I don't recall having specific issues with waiting my turn, this physical restlessness is a constant struggle for me during passive tasks.

Can you recall any instances in your past where you felt the need to be constantly moving or had trouble sitting still in situations where you were expected to be quiet, such as in church, at the dinner table, or during family gatherings?

I don't recall having significant physical restlessness or trouble sitting still in those childhood situations. Back then, my difficulties were much more focused on drifting off, losing track of details, and making careless mistakes rather than any physical hyperactivity.

You've mentioned difficulties with restlessness and fidgeting in certain situations, but can you think of any times in your life where you exhibited more overt signs of hyperactivity, such as running, climbing, or other physically active behaviors that stood out to you or others?

I don't recall ever having those kinds of overt hyperactive behaviors like running or climbing around, even when I was a child. Any restlessness I've experienced has always felt much more internal or subtle rather than physically wild.

Can you think of any times in your childhood or adolescence where others, such as parents or teachers, commented on or were concerned about your level of activity or restlessness, even if you didn't exhibit overt hyperactive behaviors?

I don't recall anyone commenting on my activity level or restlessness when I was younger. The feedback I received from teachers and parents was almost entirely about me being distracted, drifting off, or making careless mistakes rather than being physically hyperactive.

Can you think of any situations where you felt the need to be constantly active or had trouble sitting still, which might help differentiate between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, predominantly inattentive type, and other presentations?

Currently, I feel that restless need to be active during long Zoom calls where I'm mostly listening, which makes me shift in my chair, pace off-camera, or open new tabs to burn off energy. Even during quiet leisure activities like reading or sketching, I struggle to sit quietly and feel antsy within minutes unless I have a podcast playing in the background.
